name: miraDry
lead: miraDry is a non-invasive microwave device made by Miramar Labs that heats tissue in the armpit to destroy sweat glands. People use it to cut underarm sweating and odor, which shows up as drier shirts, fewer sweat marks and less underarm odor, and the same energy also damages hair follicles, so some patients see less underarm hair. It has been cleared by the US FDA (2011, per Wikipedia) and Health Canada for axillary hyperhidrosis and is also used for underarm odor.[1][2][20]

Treatment is done by a clinician: local anesthetic is injected into the armpit and the microwave emitter is applied to the skin.[3] Wikipedia reports sweat reductions of roughly 82 percent on average and underarm hair reductions of about 75 percent, with effects noticeable almost immediately and long-lasting.[20] A 2022 review of microwave technology in dermatology covers its use for axillary hyperhidrosis and osmidrosis.[1]
Several clinical studies and patient surveys have been published, and case reports document rare serious complications including brachial plexus nerve injury and a fatal infection.[3][4][6][7]

paras: The system delivers microwave energy through the skin to heat the layer where sweat glands sit. Because glands are destroyed rather than temporarily blocked, the aim is a longer-lasting effect than antiperspirants or botulinum toxin injections.[20] Published follow-up extends to three years.[15]

Patients typically receive local anesthetic in the armpit, then the handpiece is applied across a marked treatment area. Some patients receive one session and others a second; one retrospective analysis found 84 percent were treated effectively with a single treatment and 16 percent needed a second.[7] A registered trial studied axillary hair loss after treatment.[8]

The procedure targets underarm sweat stains, damp clothing and body odor (bromhidrosis or osmidrosis), and the incidental loss of hair follicles in the treated area appeals to some patients as long-term underarm hair reduction.[1][20]

It is cleared for primary axillary hyperhidrosis. Hyperhidrosis affects roughly 1 to 2 percent of the population and is most noticeable in people under 40; authors link the burden of sweat and odor to reduced quality of life.[6] A registered study also looked at microwave ablation in mild axillary hidradenitis suppurativa and was terminated with 9 participants.[14]

Wikipedia's hyperhidrosis article describes the usual options for underarm sweating. Antiperspirants containing aluminium salts are first-line, with stronger solutions or gels for hyperhidrosis, improvement over about three to five days and skin irritation as the most common side effect.[2] Botulinum toxin type A is approved for severe underarm sweating that topical agents do not control; it blocks the nerve signals to sweat glands with effects lasting roughly three to nine months, and the injections can be painful.[2]

Surgical options include removing or destroying the sweat glands by suction, curettage or laser, and endoscopic thoracic sympathectomy, which is studied mostly for hand sweating and is associated with compensatory sweating elsewhere in a large share of patients (20 to 80 percent, as cited there).[2] The same article describes miraDry as appearing promising for excessive underarm sweating while noting rare but serious reported risks, including brachial plexus injury and upper-limb paralysis.[2] People choose among these based on how long they want the effect to last and how invasive a procedure they accept.

Registered trials include a 2010 study in 31 people with hyperhidrosis,[9] a 2014 study of focal axillary hyperhidrosis that was terminated,[10] a 2020 patient satisfaction and safety study in 100 people,[11] and a 2021 trial comparing the longevity of microwave thermolysis with botulinum toxin in 30 people.[12] A 2012 trial compared a 1440 nm laser with botulinum toxin or miraDry.[13]

Published results are consistent in direction. In a retrospective comparison of 39 women with both hyperhidrosis and bromhidrosis, 17 treated with miraDry and 22 with suction-curettage, both groups showed significant drops in Hyperhidrosis Disease Severity Scale (HDSS) scores and odor level at 6 and 12 months, with no significant difference between groups.[5] A retrospective analysis of 139 patients treated from 2019 to 2023 reported significant HDSS improvement (p<0.001), with Minor iodine-starch testing before and six months after treatment.[7] A three-year follow-up of 103 patients with severe axillary hyperhidrosis treated in 2020 to 2022, with 45 responding to the survey, reported median HDSS falling from 3 to 2 and median HidroQoL quality-of-life scores from 26 to 6.[15]

A 2023 study of 15 patients used pretreatment ultrasonography and a single high-energy pass, evaluating sweat and odor at baseline, 1 month, 3 months and 1 year; it identified a 'danger zone' in 14 of 30 treated areas and discussed pretreatment factors that may lower complication risk.[4] A 2024 patient satisfaction survey is also published.[6]

Wikipedia notes rare but serious risks including upper-limb paralysis and brachial plexus injury.[16] Case reports describe brachial plexus injury after treatment in a thin 49-year-old woman[3] and a thin 19-year-old man, managed conservatively.[17] A 2022 case report describes necrotizing fasciitis with streptococcal toxic shock syndrome with a fatal outcome after treatment,[18] and another case report describes complications following microwave treatment.[19]

Authors have described a 'danger zone' for nerve injury and have discussed pretreatment assessment to reduce risk, with female gender and a small mid-upper arm circumference among factors noted in one study.[4]

timeline.event: Early registered clinical evaluations of the miraDry system in hyperhidrosis begin.[9]
Case report of bilateral brachial plexus injury published.[3]

Three-year follow-up of microwave therapy published.[15]

card.summary: A microwave device that destroys underarm sweat glands in a clinic; studied in several trials, with rare but serious nerve-injury and infection case reports.
card.note: Case reports document brachial plexus injury and one fatal infection.

quick.overview:
miraDry is an FDA-cleared microwave device used in clinics to destroy underarm sweat glands, mainly for heavy sweating and sometimes odor. Treatment is done under local anesthetic.

Several registered trials, patient surveys and a three-year follow-up have been published, alongside case reports of complications.
quick.mechanism: Microwave energy heats the tissue layer containing sweat glands, destroying them so they stop producing sweat.
quick.risks: Case reports describe brachial plexus (nerve) injury, and one fatal necrotizing fasciitis case. Authors have discussed a nerve-injury 'danger zone' and pretreatment assessment.

chain: Microwave energy heats the layer holding sweat glands
Glands are destroyed rather than temporarily blocked
Less sweat and odor, with some underarm hair loss
angle.text: Patients choose miraDry for visibly drier underarms, fewer sweat stains on clothing and less odor, with underarm hair thinning as a side effect. It is an in-clinic procedure rather than a daily product.
